summary: This standards-track document specifies several YANG modules that together form the core routing data model, a framework for configuring and managing a routing subsystem. Other YANG modules for specific routing protocols are expected to extend it. This is the NMDA-compatible version of the earlier model.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8349 defines a common YANG data model for managing routing on network devices. It organizes routes into routing information bases, represents control-plane protocols, and provides IPv4 and IPv6 extensions that other protocol models can build on.

subtitle: Provides a reusable YANG framework for configuring and inspecting routing systems.

tldr.problem: Network devices need a consistent data structure for configuring routing and exposing the routes and protocols that are active.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines generic routing, IPv4 unicast, and IPv6 unicast YANG modules with shared models for routes, routing information bases, control-plane protocols, and router advertisements.
tldr.outcome: The modules form a base that protocol-specific models can extend, and can also describe simple static-routing devices. RFC 8349 obsoletes RFC 8022.

today: RFC 8349 is a Proposed Standard for the NMDA-compatible core routing data model and obsoletes RFC 8022.

sections.title: A Shared Routing Management Model
sections.content:
RFC 8349 specifies the ietf-routing, ietf-ipv4-unicast-routing, and ietf-ipv6-unicast-routing YANG modules, plus an IPv6 router-advertisements submodule. Together, they define the core routing data model.

The model follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture. It can describe simple devices that use static routes, while its generic components are intended as a foundation for richer models covering multiple routing protocols and address families.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives network-management software a shared structure for describing routing configuration and state. Protocol-specific models can extend this structure rather than defining every basic routing concept again.

sections.title: How the Data Tree Is Organized
sections.content:
The model groups routing configuration under a routing container. It includes control-plane protocol instances and routing information bases (RIBs), which hold route lists, and an action for looking up the active route for a destination.

Some list entries are created by the device itself, while others are created through configuration. A configured entry can supplement a system-created entry, and removing that configuration does not remove the underlying system-controlled operational entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The data tree separates routing protocols, routing tables, and routes. It also distinguishes entries created by the device from entries explicitly added by an administrator.

sections.title: Routes, RIBs, and Protocols
sections.content:
A route includes a destination prefix, a route preference, and next-hop information. Lower route-preference values indicate a more preferred route when routes share a destination prefix.

Each RIB contains routes for one address family, and one RIB per supported family is marked as the default. Control-plane protocols populate RIBs; the model defines local direct and static pseudo-protocols and leaves room for additional protocol types.
sections.plainLanguage: A route says which destinations it can reach, how preferred it is, and where packets should go next. Routing protocols place routes into a RIB, the list of routes for one address family.

sections.title: Connecting to Interface and IP Models
sections.content:
The routing model works with the interface and IP YANG modules. Disabling a network-layer interface disables routing and forwarding there; separate IPv4 and IPv6 switches control each protocol family.

Configuring an IP address and prefix on an enabled interface creates a direct route for that network. The IPv6 router-advertisements submodule adds configuration for advertisement behavior and the prefixes included in those advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing configuration depends on the device's interface and IP configuration. Enabling an address on an interface also supplies a direct route for the connected network.

sections.title: Protecting Routing Management Data
sections.content:
The YANG modules are intended to be accessed through network-management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF, which use secure transport mechanisms. Access-control rules can limit which users may read or change data.

Control-plane protocol and RIB configuration can affect network operation, so write access to these data nodes needs protection. Their contents may also reveal sensitive routing details, so read access should be controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing a routing protocol or routing table can affect how a device forwards traffic. Management systems should protect both write access and access to sensitive routing information.
